title: Bidirectional BFS in Hollywood: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS runs two BFS searches—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. In a city grid pathfinding visualization, this cuts the explored search space dramatically compared to a single-direction BFS.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how launching two searches doubles speed ⚡

In a real map grid, classic BFS expands outward layer-by-layer from the start, exploring a huge wavefront. Bidirectional BFS flips the script: we BFS from START and GOAL simultaneously, expanding one “ring” from each side until the frontiers intersect (the meeting node).

✅ Why it’s faster (intuition): if the shortest path length is d and branching factor is b, single BFS explores ~b^d states. Bidirectional BFS explores roughly two searches of depth ~d/2, so the work trends toward ~2·b^(d/2) — that’s the “cuts the search space in half” idea.

🧠 Coding interview prep mechanics:
- Maintain two queues: qF (from start) and qB (from goal)
- Maintain two visited maps: visitedF and visitedB (store parents for reconstruction)
- Each step: pop from the smaller queue, expand neighbors, and check if neighbor is in the other visited map
- When fronts meet, reconstruct the path by stitching parents from both directions

📌 Takeaway: You’re not “guessing”—you’re shrinking the effective depth by meeting in the middle.

🤔 Debate question: When would Bidirectional BFS NOT help much—very small graphs, uneven branching, or when the goal isn’t known?
